title: How did a trading port bring people together?
essentialQuestion: What can a town's river, streets and buildings tell us about the people who met there, and what can they not tell us?
learningGoal: Explain how the river port of Hội An could connect people, and say what a modern photo of the town can and cannot show.

warmUp.question: Why might a town grow beside a river, close to the sea?
options: There is water for people and crops

evidence.question: Which source tells you about the old port? Which one shows the town today?

cards.title: Two real sources about Hội An

sources.caption: Source 1: UNESCO's description of Hội An Ancient Town (a modern heritage account)
details: Written by UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, for the World Heritage List. Hội An was listed in 1999.
It says Hội An was a trading port from the 1400s to the 1800s, near the mouth of the Thu Bồn River.
It describes shops and homes, an open market and a ferry quay.
It says many buildings face the street for customers, and their backs open to the river for loading boats.
It says the buildings mix local and foreign ways, mainly Chinese and Japanese, with later European ones.
Limit: it is a modern account of buildings that survive. It is not a record written by people who lived there in the 1400s.

sources.caption: Source 2: A photo of a covered bridge in Hội An, taken on 27 July 2018 by Christophe95
details: A photographer called Christophe95 took it and shared it on Wikimedia Commons.
It shows a covered bridge with a tiled roof, often called the Japanese Bridge, seen from across the river.
In front there is a lower wooden footbridge, and many visitors stand on the bank.
Limit: it shows the place in 2018. It cannot show the port's old traders or what residents thought.

events.text: Hội An is a busy trading port, according to UNESCO.
UNESCO lists Hội An Ancient Town as a World Heritage site.

sections.heading: A town by a river
sections.text: Hội An is a town in central Viet Nam, near the place where the Thu Bồn River meets the sea. From the 1400s to the 1800s, it was a busy trading port. Boats brought goods by water, and people on land sold, loaded and carried them. The river and the sea connected the town with traders from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. But not everyone in Hội An was a visiting trader. Local people built their lives there too. The town's location helps explain why a port grew there. It cannot tell us who had power, or how each family lived.
sections.simpler: Hội An is a town in Viet Nam. It is near a river and the sea. For about 400 years, it was a busy port. Boats came with goods. People on land sold and carried the goods. Traders came from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. Local people lived there too. The river helps us see why a port grew here. It does not tell us how each family lived.

sections.heading: A modern heritage account
sections.text: In 1999, UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, listed Hội An as a World Heritage site. Its description says the old town has shops, homes, an open market and a ferry quay. Many buildings face the street, so customers could walk in. Their backs open to the river, so goods could go on and off boats. From this, we can make an inference: the river and the street were both important for trade. UNESCO says the buildings mix local ways with mostly Chinese and Japanese ideas, and later European ones. This is a modern account, not a diary from a trader in the 1500s.
sections.simpler: In 1999, UNESCO listed Hội An as a special place. UNESCO is part of the United Nations. It says the town has shops, homes and a market. It has a quay by the river. Customers come in at the front of a shop. The back opens to the river, where boats load goods. So we can make an inference. The river and the street both helped trade. UNESCO wrote this in modern times. It is not a diary from long ago.

sections.heading: A bridge photographed later
sections.text: The second picture is a photo of a covered bridge in Hội An, taken in 2018. The bridge is part of the town's heritage, a place people value and look after today. The photo shows what the bridge looked like on that day. It cannot show the first traders who used the port centuries ago, or what every resident thought. The map helps us see possible connections, and the photo lets us look at a place now. To hear a resident's view from long ago, we would need other sources, such as old records or objects.
sections.simpler: The second picture is a photo of a bridge. It was taken in 2018. The bridge is part of the town's heritage. People care for it today. The photo shows the bridge on one day. It does not show the old traders. To learn about people long ago, we need other sources. Old records and objects can help.

glossary.definition: Places and ways of life that people value and care for.

glossary.definition: An idea you build from evidence and can test with more evidence.

checks.question: UNESCO says Hội An was a trading port. For how long?

options.feedback: Not quite. The port was busy for much longer than one year. Look at the dates in the first part of the reading.
Yes. UNESCO says it was a trading port from the 1400s to the 1800s. That is about 400 years.
Not quite. 1999 is when UNESCO listed the town. The trade came much earlier. Look at the first part of the reading.

checks.question: The bridge photo was taken in 2018. What can it show us?

options.feedback: Not quite. A photo from 2018 cannot show people from 1700. Check the date of the photo.
Not quite. The photo cannot show the first traders. They lived centuries before 2018. Look at the third part of the reading.

options.text: What the bridge looked like in 2018
options.feedback: Yes. The photo shows the bridge on one day in 2018. It is evidence of a place that survives today.

write.prompt: Use two details from the sources to explain how Hội An could connect people. Then write one question that the bridge photo cannot answer.
sentenceStarters: Hội An could connect people because ...
One question the photo cannot answer is ...
selfCheck: I used two details from the sources.
I explained how the port could connect people.
I wrote one question the photo cannot answer.
write.example: Hội An could connect people because it was a port near a river and the sea. UNESCO's account says the town has a market and a ferry quay. Another detail is that many shops faced the street. Their backs opened to the river, so boats could load goods there. The 2018 photo shows a covered bridge that people still look after. One question the photo cannot answer is how a trader lived there 300 years ago.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, write two questions to investigate: one about a person who lived in Hội An long ago, and one about a visiting trader. Say which source could help answer each one.
speak.independentTask: Name two groups of people who used the port. For each group, say one source you would need to learn about their lives.

watch.title: Hoi An Ancient Town (UNESCO/NHK)
watch.why: A short UNESCO and NHK film about Hội An's old town and its covered bridge, the place this lesson's sources describe.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you expect a short film about an old port town to show?
watch.afterQuestion: Name one building or street you saw in the film. Was it filmed in the trading-port years or in modern times?
watch.summary: This is a short film of a few minutes. NHK, a broadcaster from Japan, made it with UNESCO. It is part of a series of films about World Heritage sites. UNESCO's record of the film says it is about the old town and its covered bridge, often called the Japanese Bridge. The record describes Hội An in a few words. Hội An is an old trading port that has been well looked after. It was a port from the 1400s to the 1800s. Its buildings and its street plan show a mix of local ways and ideas from other places. Remember that a camera films a place on one day. The film shows Hội An in modern times, not the busy port of long ago.
keyPoints: Hội An was a trading port from the 1400s to the 1800s.
Its buildings and street plan mix local ways with ideas from other places.
The film shows the town in modern times, not the port long ago.

visual.description: A modern explanatory map-diagram of Hội An's river port, marked "modern map, simplified" in one corner. Right: the sea (pale blue), labelled "Sea". A river labelled "Thu Bồn River" runs from the left (west) into the sea (east). On the river's north bank, near the mouth, a small town block labelled "Hội An (port)". Inside the town, a simple cut-away row of buildings: the front faces a street labelled "street: customers", the back faces the river labelled "river side: loading", and a small landing at the water labelled "quay". Two small, plain figures (no faces, no costume details): one on land labelled "local residents", one beside a simple boat labelled "visiting traders". From the river mouth, three dashed arrows lead out to sea toward edge labels "Southeast Asia", "East Asia" and "later: Europe", with a key: "dashed = illustrative routes, not one ship's record". Under the map, a small timeline strip with three points: "1400s–1800s trading port", "1999 World Heritage listing", "2018 photo". No ships' names, no flags, no historical scene.
visual.alt: A simple modern map of Hội An near where the Thu Bồn River meets the sea. Buildings face a street for customers and open to the river for loading at a quay. Dashed arrows show illustrative routes to Southeast Asia, East Asia and later Europe. A timeline below shows 1400s–1800s trading port, 1999 World Heritage listing and 2018 photo.
visual.caption: A modern diagram of Hội An as a river port. The dashed routes are examples, not a record of any one ship.
visual.lookClosely: What could a river port connect, and whose work is needed on land?

secondVisual.description: Wikimedia Commons file "Japanese bridge Hoi An.jpg" by Christophe95, taken 27 July 2018: the covered bridge (Chùa Cầu, often called the Japanese Bridge) seen from across the river in Hội An, with a lower modern wooden footbridge in front and many visitors on the bank. Chosen because it is a clearly dated, real photo of a surviving part of the heritage town, which lets learners practise separating a 2018 photo from the 1400s–1800s port.
secondVisual.alt: A covered bridge with a curved tiled roof and pink walls at each end crosses a shallow river. In front is a lower wooden footbridge with a cyclist and walkers, and a crowd of visitors stands on the right bank.
secondVisual.caption: A bridge in Hội An photographed in 2018. It is evidence of a place that survives today, not a photo from the trading-port years.
secondVisual.lookClosely: What does the photo show today? What can it not prove about the people who lived here centuries ago?

sensitiveNotes: Keep the focus on Hội An's past and its sources. Never ask learners about their own or their family's journeys, home countries, ethnicity or religion; when learners imagine residents or traders, they write questions to investigate, not invented life stories.
educatorNotes: Aim: learners explain one way the port connected people, using a source detail, and name one resident's view a building-centred account leaves out. Evidence move: trace the street-to-river loading idea in UNESCO's description (buildings face the street, backs open to the river), then point to the photo's date, 2018, before learners say what it shows. A sound answer gives one supported connection and one missing resident source.

Misconception to address: that a later photo is a picture of the port's earlier daily life. Also, "Chinese and Japanese influences" in buildings do not tell us every resident's ancestry, and local people were not passive; the bridge's popular name does not tell us who built or used it. UNESCO's listing dates the wooden bridge, with a pagoda on it, to the 18th century, while other accounts give an earlier first bridge, so the lesson does not date it. Source caveats: UNESCO's account is a modern interpretation of surviving buildings; the photo shows a lower modern footbridge in front and crowds of visitors in 2018. For an optional comparison with another port that records local voices, see George Town World Heritage Incorporated's oral history work, but do not make it a second case.
changes: Written on 1 November 2026 from Justin's course brief (28 October 2026), sections 3 and 3A.

Followed the brief's checks: the first asks how long Hội An was a port (several centuries); the second asks what a 2018 photo can show. The 3A check about UNESCO's account being modern is taught in Read part 2 and in the evidence card instead.
Wrote "from the 1400s to the 1800s" for UNESCO's "15th to the 19th century", which is easier to read. Said "about 400 years" in the simpler text and the check feedback.

Checked UNESCO's listing on 1 November 2026 for the location (north bank, near the mouth of the Thu Bồn River), the dates (15th to 19th century), the buildings, the street-to-river layout and the influences. The 1999 inscription is now confirmed from UNESCO's own decision page (23 COM VIII.C.1, 1999), added to sources.
Softened 3A's "cared for and repaired over time" to "value and look after today": I could not confirm repair dates from a source I opened.

Commons file checked through the Commons API on 1 November 2026: Christophe95, taken 27 July 2018, own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, as the brief says. Its description names the bridge "The Japanese bridge (Chùa Cầu)". Alt text written from the image itself: it also shows a modern wooden footbridge in front and many visitors.

Added an English Watch step (the team now allows English videos): Hoi An Ancient Town (UNESCO/NHK), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0BIcOTSD9k, the brief's section 5 candidate, from UNESCO's own channel; title and channel confirmed with oEmbed. The summary rests only on UNESCO's archive record, as the captions could not be read. Someone must watch it before learners see it.
